scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The cakewalk originated in the mid-19th century among enslaved African Americans on Southern U.S. plantations, especially Florida, as a satirical imitation of white slaveholders' formal dances.
It evolved from 'prize walks' where dancers competed for a cake.
Firsthand accounts describe elaborate nighttime parties with music and dance, attended by slaveowners who judged the contests.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally danced at plantation gatherings, especially on Sundays or winter evenings when work was light, the cakewalk was both entertainment and covert satire of slaveholder culture.
It was a social event for enslaved people to express joy, creativity, and resistance.
After emancipation, it became a popular stage performance and social dance across the U.S. and Europe.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Cakewalk music is generally in 2/4 time with a syncopated 'oom-pah' rhythm featuring two alternate heavy beats per bar.
It incorporates polyrhythm, syncopation, and habanera rhythm patterns.
Listen for the banjo, violin, jaw harp, piano.
The pulse is 2/4.
Bright, rhythmic march with syncopated beats and lively tempo, featuring banjo and piano with playful, accented rhythms that support strutting dance steps.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wore discarded finery such as top hats, tailcoats, wide bow ties, canes, hoop skirts, and long dresses with ruffles, emulating and mocking the formal attire of white slaveholders.
Performances took place at plantation gatherings, community parties, minstrel shows, and later on Broadway stages and music halls.
Settings ranged from outdoor plantation yards to large urban theaters.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Charles E. Johnson and his wife Dora Dean were celebrated cakewalk performers who popularized the dance on stage in the 1890s.
Entertainer Tom Fletcher documented early versions of the dance.
The cakewalk originated in Florida and spread through the Southern U.S. states including Georgia, Louisiana, and Virginia before reaching New York and Europe.
The cakewalk descends from African American ring shout dances and European couple dances like the Grand March.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Cakewalk is parent of Ring Shout: African-derived dance influencing cakewalk's footwork and call-and-response singing.
Cakewalk is shares music of Ragtime: Cakewalk rhythms influenced ragtime music and dance styles.
Cakewalk is child of Minstrel Show Dance: Cakewalk was adapted into minstrel shows, evolving in style and performance.
Cakewalk is descendant of Lindy Hop: Modern swing dance communities preserve cakewalk elements in performances.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Dancers wore discarded finery such as top hats, tailcoats, wide bow ties, canes, hoop skirts, and long dresses with ruffles, emulating and mocking the formal attire of white slaveholders. Performances took place at plantation gatherings, community parties, minstrel shows, and later on Broadway stages and music halls. Settings ranged from outdoor plantation yards to large urban theaters. The dance was often competitive, with judges awarding cakes to the best performers.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Originally danced at plantation gatherings, especially on Sundays or winter evenings when work was light, the cakewalk was both entertainment and covert satire of slaveholder culture. It was a social event for enslaved people to express joy, creativity, and resistance. After emancipation, it became a popular stage performance and social dance across the U.S. and Europe. The cakewalk's meaning shifted from subtle mockery to a grotesque caricature in minstrel shows, though its origins as a dignified parody remain central to its identity.
